learn.hook: Lifting a bucket up a well stores energy that does not care which staircase you take. Electric forces behave the same way, which lets us define electric potential.
points: The electrostatic (Coulomb) force is conservative: the work it does depends only on the start and end points, not on the path.
So we can define electric potential energy U. Work done by an external force in moving a charge slowly (no change in kinetic energy) from P to R equals U(R) - U(P).
Only differences in U are physical; we usually choose U = 0 at infinity.
Electric potential V at a point = work done by an external force per unit positive test charge in bringing it slowly from infinity to that point: V = W/q.
Like height in a building, the zero of potential is a choice. Only potential differences can be measured and matter physically.

example.q: An external agent does 6 × 10⁻⁵ J of work to bring a charge of 2 µC slowly from infinity to point P. Find the potential at P.

learn.reallife: A Mumbai local train climbing from a station to a flyover gains the same potential energy whichever route it uses; charges in a circuit gain or lose energy in the same path-independent way.

options: Because the force is very strong
Because the electrostatic force is conservative

quiz.q: Why do we bring the test charge 'slowly' when defining potential?
options: So that the charge does not lose mass
So that the field becomes uniform
So that the charge is not quantised
So that no kinetic energy is gained and all work goes into potential energy
quiz.explain: Moving it without acceleration means the external force just balances the electric force.
steps: Moving slowly means no acceleration and no gain of kinetic energy
Then the external force just balances the field and all work becomes U

quiz.q: Which of these is physically meaningful in electrostatics?
options: The absolute potential at a point without a reference
The potential energy of a single charge without a reference
The value of potential at infinity
The potential difference between two points
quiz.explain: Adding a constant to all potentials changes nothing physical; only differences matter.
steps: Adding a constant to all potentials changes nothing physical
So only potential differences can be measured

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The work done by an electrostatic field in moving a charge around a closed loop is zero. Reason (R): The electrostatic force is conservative. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

steps: A: work by the field round a closed loop is zero – true

Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not link closed-loop work with conservative force

revise.summary: The electrostatic force is conservative, so electric potential energy can be defined; only its differences matter. Electric potential V is the work per unit positive charge to bring a test charge slowly from infinity: V = W/q.

traps: Don't drop the sign of q when finding work
Absolute potential has no meaning without a reference

topics.title: Potential due to a point charge

learn.hook: A nucleus creates a potential 'hill'. Climbing it with a positive charge costs energy, and the hill gets taller as 1/r the closer you get.
points: Potential difference V_B - V_A = work per unit positive charge from A to B. Unit: volt, 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.
Integrating E = kQ/r² from infinity to r gives V(r) = Q/(4πε₀r) = kQ/r.
V is positive for positive Q and negative for negative Q, and it falls off as 1/r (slower than E ∝ 1/r²).
Work to bring q from infinity to a point at potential V: W = qV.
For two opposite charges, V = 0 at points where kq₁/r₁ + kq₂/r₂ = 0, which lies between them and also outside, beyond the smaller charge.

example.q: Find the potential 12 cm from a charge of 6 × 10⁻⁷ C. How much work brings a 3 × 10⁻⁹ C charge there from infinity?

learn.reallife: The 'Danger 11000 V' boards on Indian power poles are about potential: a large potential difference means each coulomb of charge carries a lot of energy through anything that bridges it.

quiz.mistake: Makes a power-of-ten error

quiz.explain: V = W/q, so 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'The field drops as 1/r², does the potential drop the same way?'
teach.praise: Chirp! V = kQ/r goes as 1/r, slower than the field's 1/r². Super clear!
teach.nudge: Nearly! Write the formula for V of a point charge. What power of r is in it?

revise.summary: A point charge Q gives potential V = kQ/r, positive for positive and negative for negative Q, falling as 1/r. Work to bring q from infinity is W = qV, and for opposite charges V = 0 at one point between them and one beyond the smaller charge.
traps: V ∝ 1/r, not 1/r²
For opposite charges the outside zero is not beyond the larger charge; it lies beyond the smaller one

learn.hook: Potential is a scalar. No arrows, no components: just add numbers with signs. That makes it the friendliest tool in electrostatics.
points: Superposition: V at a point due to many charges = algebraic sum k(q₁/r₁ + q₂/r₂ + ...).
Dipole potential (r ≫ a): V = p cosθ/(4πε₀r²), where θ is the angle between p and the position vector.
On the axis (θ = 0 or 180°) V = ±kp/r², the largest magnitude; on the equatorial plane (θ = 90°) V = 0.
Dipole potential depends on direction (θ) as well as distance, and falls as 1/r², faster than a point charge's 1/r.
For charges at the corners of a regular polygon, every charge is the same distance from the centre, so V(centre) = k(Σq)/r.

example.q: Charges of +2 µC, +2 µC, -1 µC and +1 µC sit at the corners of a square, each 0.3 m from the centre. Find V at the centre.

learn.reallife: Doctors reading an ECG at AIIMS are looking at potential differences produced by the heart, which behaves roughly like a rotating electric dipole as it beats.

quiz.q: Why is it often easier to find the potential than the field due to several charges?

Potential is a scalar, so contributions add algebraically

Potential is a scalar: contributions just add with signs

quiz.q: Assertion (A): At points on the equatorial plane of a dipole, the potential is zero but the field is not. Reason (R): Potential is a scalar sum, while the field is a vector sum. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Equal and opposite potentials cancel as numbers; the fields' components along the axis add instead of cancelling.
steps: A: on the equatorial plane V = 0 but E ≠ 0 – true
R: V is a scalar sum, E a vector sum – true
+kq/r and −kq/r cancel as numbers, but the fields' components add; R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Assumes zero potential means zero field

teach.praise: Chirp! Zero potential, but the vector fields add up along -p. Potential and field are different things!
teach.nudge: Good! Is potential a vector or a scalar? What about the field?

revise.summary: Potentials of several charges add as scalars. A short dipole has V = kp cosθ/r²: ±kp/r² on the axis and zero on the equatorial plane, falling as 1/r². For a regular polygon, V(centre) = kΣq/r.

Potential at the centre of symmetric arrangements
traps: Add potentials with signs, not as vectors

learn.hook: Contour lines on a hill map join points of equal height. Bunched-up contours mean a steep slope. Equipotential surfaces do the same for electric fields.
points: An equipotential surface has the same potential at every point, so no work is done in moving a charge along it.
The electric field is always normal to equipotential surfaces (otherwise a component along the surface would do work).
Shapes: concentric spheres for a point charge, parallel planes perpendicular to a uniform field; distorted shapes for a dipole and for two like charges.
E = -dV/dl: the field points in the direction of steepest decrease of potential, with magnitude |ΔV|/Δl measured normal to the equipotentials.
Closely spaced equipotentials mean a strong field; widely spaced ones mean a weak field.

example.q: Two equipotential planes 5 cm apart differ by 10 V. Find E.
steps: = 200 V m⁻¹, from the higher to the lower potential

learn.reallife: Survey of India's topographic maps show height contours; electrical engineers draw equipotential maps around substations to keep 'step voltage' safe for people walking nearby.

The electric field can be parallel to an equipotential surface.

Because the surface is a conductor
quiz.explain: Zero work along the surface means zero field component along it.

A field component along the surface would do work
So E has no component along the surface: it is normal to it

quiz.explain: E = ΔV/Δl; smaller Δl for the same ΔV gives larger E.
steps: Same ΔV over a smaller Δl gives a larger E
quiz.mistake: Inverts the spacing-strength link

planes parallel to the x-y plane

Answer: planes parallel to the y-z plane

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Two equipotential surfaces never intersect. Reason (R): At an intersection point, the potential would have two different values. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is false but R is true

steps: A: equipotential surfaces never intersect – true
R: at an intersection V would have two values – true

Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Which way does the electric field point compared to equipotential surfaces?'
teach.praise: Chirp! E is normal to equipotentials, pointing from high to low potential. And no work along them!
teach.nudge: Close! Think about the work done along an equipotential. What does that say about E's direction?

revise.summary: An equipotential surface has the same potential everywhere, so no work is done along it and E is normal to it. E = −dV/dl points towards decreasing potential, and closely spaced equipotentials mean a strong field.
remember: Point charge: spheres; uniform field: parallel planes
traps: E does not point towards higher potential; it points from higher to lower
Don't calculate non-zero work along an equipotential; it is zero

topics.title: Potential energy of a system of charges

learn.hook: To pack charges into a tiny space you must fight their repulsion. That fight stores energy, like compressing a spring, and nuclear fission later releases it.
points: Two charges: U = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r₁₂) = kq₁q₂/r₁₂, the work needed to assemble them from infinity.
Like charges: U > 0 (work must be done to push them together). Unlike charges: U < 0 (they attract, so work is released).
Three or more charges: add U for every pair, U = k(q₁q₂/r₁₂ + q₁q₃/r₁₃ + q₂q₃/r₂₃).
Work by an external agent to change a configuration = U(final) - U(initial).
Four charges at the corners of a square have six pairs: four sides and two diagonals.

example.q: Find the work needed to place three charges of 1 µC each at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 0.1 m.

learn.reallife: Inside a uranium nucleus in a reactor at Kudankulam or Tarapur, protons are packed so tightly that their Coulomb potential energy is enormous. When the nucleus splits, part of that energy is released.

teach.nudge: Good start! What do we calculate for each pair of charges, and then what do we do?

revise.summary: The potential energy of two charges is U = kq₁q₂/r, the work to assemble them from infinity; it is positive for like and negative for unlike charges. For many charges add U for every pair; external work = U(final) − U(initial).
focus: U for a pair and its sign
traps: Don't drop the sign of each charge
Don't forget diagonal pairs in a square

topics.title: Potential energy in an external field and the electron volt

learn.hook: An electron accelerated through a single volt gains a tiny 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Physicists liked that unit so much they gave it a name: the electron volt.
points: A charge q at a point where an external potential is V(r) has potential energy qV(r). The external field's sources are taken as fixed.
Electron volt: energy gained by an electron (or lost) when it moves through a potential difference of 1 V. 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Also keV, MeV.
A charge q accelerated through ΔV gains kinetic energy qΔV.
Two charges q₁, q₂ in an external field: U = q₁V(r₁) + q₂V(r₂) + kq₁q₂/r₁₂. The last term is their mutual energy.
An electron (negative) gains energy moving towards higher potential; a proton gains energy moving towards lower potential.

example.q: A proton is accelerated from rest through 1000 V. Find its kinetic energy in eV and J.

learn.reallife: Old CRT televisions, still found in some Indian homes, accelerated electrons through about 20 kV, giving each one roughly 20 keV of energy before it hit the screen to make it glow.

quiz.q: Which statement is correct about an electron released from rest in an electric field?
options: It moves towards higher potential and gains kinetic energy
quiz.explain: For negative charge U = -eV falls as V rises, so it moves to higher V.
steps: U falls as V rises, so it moves towards higher potential
Its U turns into kinetic energy

quiz.q: An electron volt is

a unit of potential equal to 1 V
the potential at 1 m from an electron

1 eV = energy gained by an electron through 1 V = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
Answer: the energy gained by an electron moving through a potential difference of 1 V

teach.nudge: Good! Is the eV a unit of potential or of energy? How is it defined?

revise.summary: A charge q at external potential V has energy qV; accelerating through ΔV gives kinetic energy qΔV. 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; for two charges in an external field, add their mutual energy kq₁q₂/r₁₂.

System of two charges in an external field

topics.title: Potential energy of a dipole in a field

learn.hook: A compass needle settles pointing north and wobbles back if nudged. A dipole in an electric field has the same favourite direction, set by its potential energy.
points: Potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field: U(θ) = -pE cosθ = -p·E (taking U = 0 at θ = 90°).
θ = 0 (p along E): U = -pE, minimum, stable equilibrium.
θ = 180° (p opposite E): U = +pE, maximum, unstable equilibrium.
Work done by an external agent to rotate a dipole from θ₁ to θ₂: W = pE(cosθ₁ - cosθ₂).
Turning a dipole from stable (0°) to unstable (180°) needs W = 2pE.

example.q: A dipole p = 2 × 10⁻²⁹ C m is in a field of 10⁶ N C⁻¹. Find the work to turn it from 0° to 90°.

learn.reallife: Liquid crystal displays in phones assembled in Noida rely on molecular dipoles: applying a field rotates them to their minimum-energy orientation, switching pixels on and off.

games.title: Stable or not?
items: A dipole aligned along the field is in stable equilibrium.
U is minimum at θ = 0.
A dipole antiparallel to the field feels a large torque.
At 180° the torque pE sinθ is zero, though equilibrium is unstable.
U = -pE cosθ.
That is the standard expression.
Work to rotate a dipole from 90° to 0° is positive.
U falls from 0 to -pE, so the external work is -pE (the field does the work).
The potential energy of a dipole is maximum at θ = 180°.
U = +pE there.

quiz.q: A dipole p = 5 × 10⁻⁹ C m is at θ = 0° in a field of 2 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. What is its potential energy (in units of 10⁻⁴ J)?
quiz.mistake: Drops the minus sign

quiz.q: How much work is needed to rotate a dipole of p = 10⁻⁸ C m from θ = 0° to 180° in a field of 5 × 10³ N C⁻¹ (in units of 10⁻⁵ J)?
quiz.mistake: Uses pE instead of 2pE

quiz.q: In which orientation is an electric dipole in unstable equilibrium in a uniform field?
quiz.explain: At 180° torque is zero but U is maximum, so any tilt makes it rotate away.
steps: Torque is zero there, but any tilt rotates it away
quiz.mistake: Thinks perpendicular is an equilibrium

quiz.q: A molecule with p = 10⁻²⁹ C m is turned from θ = 0° to θ = 60° in a field of 10⁶ N C⁻¹. What work is needed (in units of 10⁻²⁴ J)?
quiz.mistake: Uses sin 60° in place of cos 60°

quiz.q: The expression U = -p·E for a dipole assumes U = 0 when
quiz.explain: -pE cos 90° = 0, so the reference is θ = 90°.
steps: Answer: p is perpendicular to E
quiz.mistake: Thinks the reference is at θ = 0

quiz.q: At which angle are both the torque and the potential energy of the dipole zero?
options: No angle: U = 0 at 90°, where the torque is maximum
quiz.explain: U = 0 at 90°, where τ = pE is maximum; τ = 0 at 0° and 180°, where U = ∓pE ≠ 0.
steps: U = 0 only at 90°, where τ = pE sin90° is maximum
τ = 0 only at 0° and 180°, where U = ∓pE ≠ 0
So they are never both zero
Answer: No angle: U = 0 at 90°, where the torque is maximum
quiz.mistake: Assumes torque and energy vanish together

quiz.q: A dipole in a field of 10⁴ N C⁻¹ has a potential energy of -3 × 10⁻⁵ J when aligned with the field. What is p (in nC m)?
quiz.explain: U = -pE, so p = 3 × 10⁻⁵/10⁴ = 3 × 10⁻⁹ C m = 3 nC m.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the negative sign in p

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A dipole placed in a uniform field tends to align with the field. Reason (R): Its potential energy is minimum when p is along E. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Systems move towards minimum potential energy; the torque rotates p into line with E.
steps: A: a dipole tends to align with the field – true
R: U is minimum when p is along E – true
Systems move to minimum U, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not relate the torque to the energy minimum

teach.ask: Gappu tilted a dipole in a field: 'Why does it swing back to point along the field?'
teach.praise: Chirp! U = -pE cosθ is lowest at θ = 0, and the torque turns it back there. Stable!
teach.nudge: Nice! Where is the dipole's potential energy lowest, and what pushes it there?

revise.summary: A dipole in a uniform field has U = −pE cosθ, minimum (stable) when p is along E and maximum (unstable) when opposite. Work to rotate it from θ₁ to θ₂ is pE(cosθ₁ − cosθ₂).
traps: U = 0 at 90°, not at 0°
Use cosθ₁ − cosθ₂, not the reverse

learn.hook: Copper is full of free electrons. Put it in a field and they rush around until they have cancelled the field inside. That simple fact gives conductors five superpowers.
points: Inside a conductor (in electrostatic equilibrium) the field is zero; free charges rearrange until the internal field vanishes.
Just outside, the field is normal to the surface; a tangential part would push charges along the surface.
There is no net charge in the interior; any excess charge sits on the outer surface.
The whole conductor (inside and surface) is at one potential: it is an equipotential volume.
Just outside, E = (σ/ε₀) n̂, with σ the local surface charge density and n̂ the outward normal.

example.q: A conducting surface has σ = 2.6 × 10⁻⁶ C m⁻². Find the field just outside. (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
steps: ≈ 2.9 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹, normal to the surface
example.answer: ≈ 2.9 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹, outward along the normal

learn.reallife: Metal cabinets of ATMs and server racks in Bengaluru data centres stay at one potential and are earthed, so stray charge never builds up across the electronics inside.

Free charges cancel any internal field.
Excess charge on a conductor spreads evenly through its volume.
It lives on the outer surface.

A tangential component would move charges.
Different points on the surface of a charged conductor can be at different potentials.
The conductor is an equipotential.
The field just outside a conductor is σ/(2ε₀).
For a conductor it is σ/ε₀; σ/(2ε₀) is for a thin sheet.

Electrons drift opposite to the field

options: Only at its sharpest point and nowhere else
quiz.explain: Gauss's law with E = 0 inside shows no charge in the interior.
steps: E = 0 inside, so a Gaussian surface just inside encloses no charge
Excess charge must sit on the outer surface

quiz.q: A charged conductor has potential 200 V at its surface. What is the potential at its centre (in V)?

quiz.q: Why is the electrostatic field at the surface of a conductor normal to it?
options: Any tangential component would move surface charges, so equilibrium needs it to vanish
Because the field inside is non-zero
quiz.explain: In equilibrium charges are at rest, so no force along the surface.
steps: In equilibrium surface charges are at rest
A tangential field would push them along the surface
So only the normal component remains
Answer: Any tangential component would move surface charges, so equilibrium needs it to vanish
quiz.mistake: Gives a geometric rather than a physical reason

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is an equipotential. Reason (R): The field inside and the tangential field on its surface are zero. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: With no field along any path within or on the conductor, no work is done, so V is the same everywhere.
steps: A: a conductor in equilibrium is an equipotential – true
R: field inside and tangential field on surface are zero – true
No field along any path ⇒ no work ⇒ same V; R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Misses the link between zero field and constant potential

quiz.q: The surface charge density at a point on a conductor is doubled. The field just outside that point
quiz.explain: E = σ/ε₀ is proportional to σ.
quiz.mistake: Thinks E depends on σ²

quiz.q: A neutral metal slab is placed in a uniform external field. Which statement is correct?
options: Negative charge appears on the face where the field enters and positive on the face where it leaves
Positive charge appears where the field enters
quiz.explain: Electrons drift against the field to the entry face; the other face is left positive. Their field cancels the external field inside.
steps: Free electrons drift opposite to E, towards the face where the field enters
That face becomes negative; the exit face is left positive
Their field cancels the external field inside
Answer: Negative charge appears on the face where the field enters and positive on the face where it leaves
quiz.mistake: Reverses the induced charges

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why is there no electric field inside a metal spoon kept near a charged comb?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Free electrons shift to the surface until their field cancels the outside field inside the metal. Smart!
teach.nudge: Good! What do the free electrons in the metal do when a field acts on them?

revise.summary: In electrostatic equilibrium the field inside a conductor is zero, excess charge lies on its outer surface, the field just outside is normal with E = σ/ε₀, and the whole conductor is an equipotential.
focus: Induced charges in an external field
remember: E = 0 inside; no charge in the interior
Field at surface is normal; E = σ/ε₀
traps: V inside is not zero; it equals the surface potential
Electrons do not gather where the field leaves; they gather on the face where it enters

topics.title: Shielding, sharp points and charged shells

learn.hook: During a thunderstorm on the Mumbai-Pune expressway, the safest place is inside your car. The metal body acts as an electrostatic shield.
points: Electrostatic shielding: the field inside any empty cavity of a conductor is zero, whatever the outside fields or charges. Sensitive instruments are kept in metal enclosures.

Charge on a conductor concentrates where the surface is most curved (sharp points), giving large σ and large fields; air can break down there (corona discharge). Lightning conductors use sharp points.
Charge q placed inside a cavity of a neutral conducting shell induces -q on the cavity wall and +q on the outer surface.
Uniformly charged shell of radius R: V = kq/r outside (r ≥ R) and V = kq/R, constant, everywhere inside.
Inside the shell E = 0 but V is not zero; it equals the surface potential.

example.q: A shell of radius 0.1 m carries 2 nC. Find V at its centre and at 0.3 m from the centre.
example.answer: 180 V at the centre; 60 V at 0.3 m

learn.reallife: Tall buildings in Kolkata and temple towers often carry a pointed copper lightning conductor connected to an earthed plate. The point helps discharge build-up, and the conductor guides strikes safely to the ground.

games.title: Shielding facts
items: The field inside a cavity in a conductor is zero even when there are charges outside the conductor.
That is electrostatic shielding.
Charge density is greatest at the flattest part of a conductor.
It is greatest at sharp, highly curved parts.
The potential inside a charged hollow shell is zero.
It is constant and equal to kq/R.
A charge q inside a cavity induces -q on the cavity wall.
So that the field inside the conductor's material is zero.
Sitting inside a car during lightning is safer than standing in an open field.
The metal body shields the inside.

quiz.q: A thin shell of radius 0.2 m carries 4 nC. What is the potential at a point 0.1 m from its centre (in V)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
quiz.explain: Inside the shell V is constant and equal to kq/R = 36/0.2 = 180 V.
steps: Inside a shell V is constant = kq/R
quiz.mistake: Uses the distance from the centre instead of R, or takes V = 0 inside

quiz.q: For the same shell (4 nC, R = 0.2 m), what is the potential at 0.4 m from the centre (in V)?
quiz.explain: Outside V = kq/r = 36/0.4 = 90 V.
quiz.mistake: Divides by r²

quiz.q: Why does a lightning conductor have pointed tips?
options: Charge density and field are very high at sharp points, so charge leaks away into the air
quiz.explain: High σ at points gives strong fields that ionise air, enabling discharge.
steps: Charge crowds at sharp points, so σ and E = σ/ε₀ are very large there
The strong field ionises air and charge leaks away safely
Answer: Charge density and field are very high at sharp points, so charge leaks away into the air
quiz.mistake: Thinks charge avoids sharp regions

quiz.q: A charge +q is placed at the centre of a cavity in a neutral conducting sphere. What charges appear on the inner and outer surfaces?
options: -q on the inner surface, +q on the outer surface
quiz.explain: The inner wall gets -q so that E = 0 in the metal; the outer surface gets +q since the conductor is neutral overall.
steps: E = 0 in the metal ⇒ inner wall must carry −q
The shell is neutral, so the outer surface gets +q
Answer: -q on the inner surface, +q on the outer surface
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the conductor stays neutral overall

quiz.q: Which is the best example of electrostatic shielding?
options: Keeping a sensitive instrument inside a closed metal box
Using a long copper wire as an antenna
quiz.explain: The field inside a closed conducting enclosure is zero.
steps: The field inside a closed conducting enclosure is zero
So a metal box shields an instrument from outside fields
Answer: Keeping a sensitive instrument inside a closed metal box
quiz.mistake: Confuses insulation with shielding

quiz.q: A conducting sphere of radius 9 cm has a potential of 200 V at its surface. What is the charge on it (in nC)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
quiz.mistake: Uses R in cm without converting

quiz.q: A hollow conducting sphere carries charge Q₁. A small charge Q₂ is placed at its centre. The field outside the sphere at distance r from the centre is
quiz.explain: The outer surface ends up with Q₁ + Q₂ (the original Q₁ plus the induced +Q₂), so Gauss's law gives k(Q₁ + Q₂)/r².
steps: Q₂ at the centre induces −Q₂ on the inner surface and +Q₂ on the outer
Gauss's law outside: E = k(Q₁ + Q₂)/r²
quiz.mistake: Ignores the induced charge on the outer surface

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Corona discharge is seen near sharp points of high-voltage conductors. Reason (R): Surface charge density is larger at points of smaller radius of curvature. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.explain: Large σ means large field σ/ε₀, which ionises the surrounding air.
steps: A: corona discharge occurs near sharp points – true
R: σ is larger where radius of curvature is smaller – true
Large σ ⇒ large field σ/ε₀ ⇒ air ionises; R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not link curvature with charge density

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If lightning hits a car, why are people inside safe?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The metal body is a conducting shell: charge stays on the outside and the field inside is zero. Safe!
teach.nudge: Good! What is special about the field inside a closed conductor?

revise.summary: The field inside a conductor's cavity is zero (electrostatic shielding). Charge concentrates at sharp points, causing corona discharge; a charge in a cavity induces −q inside and +q outside; a shell has V = kq/R inside and kq/r outside.
focus: Charge at sharp points and lightning conductors
Charges induced by a charge in a cavity; shell potential
remember: Shell: V = kq/R inside (constant), kq/r outside
Charge q in cavity → −q on inner wall, +q on outer surface
traps: Inside a shell V is not zero, though E = 0
Sharp points have higher, not lower, σ

learn.hook: Put a slab of glass between charged plates and the field inside weakens. The glass has no free electrons, yet it fights back. How?
points: Dielectrics are insulators. Unlike conductors, they have no free charges, but their molecules get polarised in a field, which only partly reduces the field inside.
Polar molecules (e.g. H₂O) have permanent dipoles that align with the field; non-polar molecules get induced dipoles by charge separation.
Polarisation P = dipole moment per unit volume. For linear dielectrics P = χe E, where χe is the electric susceptibility.
A uniformly polarised slab acquires bound surface charges ±σp on its faces. These produce a field opposite to the applied one, so the field inside is reduced (not cancelled).
Contrast: inside a conductor E becomes exactly zero; inside a dielectric E is only reduced.

example.q: A slab is placed in a uniform field E₀. Its bound charges produce an opposing field of E₀/4. Find the net field inside.
steps: The dielectric reduces but does not cancel the field

learn.reallife: Mica and ceramic are used as insulating dielectrics in capacitors on the circuit boards of Indian-made smartphones and EV chargers.

games.title: Dielectric facts
items: A dielectric placed in a field has zero field inside, like a conductor.
The field is reduced, not cancelled.
Polarisation is the dipole moment per unit volume.
That is its definition.
Non-polar molecules can become dipoles in an external field.
These are induced dipoles.
Bound surface charges on a polarised slab can flow away if touched by a wire.
Bound charges are tied to molecules; they are not free.
The field due to bound charges inside the slab opposes the applied field.
That is why the net field is reduced.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a conductor and a dielectric placed in an electric field?
options: Both make the field zero inside
A dielectric increases the field inside
The field inside a conductor becomes zero, but inside a dielectric it is only reduced
A conductor only reduces the field
quiz.explain: Free charges in a conductor cancel the field; bound charges in a dielectric only partly oppose it.
steps: Conductor: free charges cancel the field, so E inside = 0
Dielectric: bound charges only partly oppose it
Answer: The field inside a conductor becomes zero, but inside a dielectric it is only reduced
quiz.mistake: Treats a dielectric like a conductor

quiz.q: Polarisation P of a dielectric is defined as
quiz.explain: P = total dipole moment / volume.

Answer: dipole moment per unit volume
quiz.mistake: Confuses polarisation with surface charge density

quiz.q: In the relation P = χe E, the quantity χe is called the
quiz.explain: χe measures how strongly a material polarises in response to the field.
steps: P = χe E for a linear dielectric
quiz.mistake: Confuses susceptibility with dielectric strength

quiz.q: A non-polar molecule placed in an electric field
options: develops an induced dipole moment along the field
gets a permanent dipole moment opposite to the field
quiz.explain: The field pushes the nucleus and electron cloud apart, inducing a dipole along E.
steps: The field pushes the nucleus and electron cloud apart
This creates an induced dipole along E
Answer: develops an induced dipole moment along the field
quiz.mistake: Thinks the molecule gains net charge

quiz.q: Why do polar molecules not show any net polarisation without an external field?
options: Their dipoles always cancel inside each molecule
Their permanent dipoles point in random directions due to thermal motion
They are all aligned opposite to each other in pairs
quiz.explain: Random orientations average out; an applied field partly aligns them.
steps: Each polar molecule has a permanent dipole
Thermal motion points them in random directions, so they average to zero
Answer: Their permanent dipoles point in random directions due to thermal motion

quiz.q: A dielectric slab in an applied field E₀ has a net internal field of 0.2E₀. What field do its bound charges produce (in terms of E₀, opposing)?
quiz.explain: Net = E₀ - E_bound, so E_bound = E₀ - 0.2E₀ = 0.8E₀.
quiz.mistake: Gives the net field instead of the bound-charge field

quiz.q: Where do the bound charges of a uniformly polarised dielectric slab appear?
options: On its two faces perpendicular to the field
On the faces parallel to the field
quiz.explain: Inside, neighbouring dipole charges cancel; only the end faces have uncancelled bound charge.
steps: Only the two faces perpendicular to the field keep uncancelled bound charge
Answer: On its two faces perpendicular to the field
quiz.mistake: Puts the bound charge in the volume

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A dielectric reduces the field between capacitor plates. Reason (R): Bound charges on its surfaces produce a field opposing the applied field. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The opposing field of the induced surface charges reduces the net field.
steps: A: a dielectric reduces the field between plates – true
R: bound surface charges produce an opposing field – true
That opposing field is the cause, so R explains A
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not see how bound charges create an opposing field

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Glass has no free electrons. How can it weaken an electric field?'
teach.praise: Chirp! The molecules become dipoles, bound surface charges appear, and their field opposes the applied one. Wow!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens to the molecules of glass in a field, and what charges appear on its surfaces?

revise.summary: Dielectrics have no free charges but polarise in a field: polar molecules align and non-polar ones get induced dipoles. Polarisation P = χeE creates bound surface charges whose opposing field reduces, but does not cancel, the field inside.
remember: P = dipole moment per unit volume = χeE
Bound charges appear on faces perpendicular to E
Net field = applied − bound field (reduced, not zero)

Polar molecules show no net P without a field

learn.hook: A camera flash charges up in a second and fires its energy in a millisecond. The little device that holds that charge is a capacitor.
points: A capacitor is two conductors separated by an insulator, carrying charges +Q and -Q.
Capacitance C = Q/V, where V is the potential difference between the plates. Unit: farad (1 F = 1 C V⁻¹). Practical units: µF (10⁻⁶ F), nF (10⁻⁹ F), pF (10⁻¹² F).
C depends only on the geometry (size, shape, separation) and the medium between the conductors, not on Q or V.
Too high a voltage makes the field exceed the dielectric strength (about 3 × 10⁶ V m⁻¹ for air), and the medium breaks down. Circuit symbol: two parallel lines.
Parallel plate capacitor: field between the plates is σ/ε₀ (σ = Q/A) and practically zero outside, ignoring fringing at the edges.

example.q: A capacitor stores 60 µC when connected to a 12 V supply. Find C. What charge does it hold at 24 V?
steps: C does not change with V
example.answer: C = 5 µF; Q = 120 µC at 24 V

learn.reallife: The ceiling fans in most Indian homes use a 2–4 µF capacitor to help the motor start; when a fan hums but will not spin, a technician often replaces this capacitor.

Capacitance depends on the medium between the plates.
A dielectric increases C.
Between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor, E = σ/ε₀.
The two sheet fields add.
Outside an ideal parallel plate capacitor, E = σ/ε₀.
Outside, the fields cancel to zero.
If the voltage across a capacitor is too high, the dielectric can break down.
The field exceeds the dielectric strength.

quiz.explain: C depends on geometry and medium only; Q doubles instead.
steps: C depends only on geometry and medium
Doubling V doubles Q; C = Q/V is unchanged
quiz.mistake: Thinks C depends on V

quiz.q: A parallel plate capacitor's plates have σ = 17.7 × 10⁻⁹ C m⁻². What is the field between them (in V m⁻¹)? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
quiz.mistake: Uses σ/2ε₀

quiz.q: Why is there a maximum safe voltage rating printed on a capacitor?
options: Above it, the plates melt from current flow
Above it, the field in the dielectric exceeds its dielectric strength and the dielectric breaks down
quiz.explain: Breakdown ionises the insulator and lets charge leak across.
steps: Field in the dielectric E = V/d rises with voltage
Above the rating E exceeds the dielectric strength and the dielectric breaks down

topics.title: Parallel plate capacitor with and without dielectric

learn.hook: How big would a 1 farad parallel plate capacitor with a 1 cm air gap be? Larger than many Indian cities! The farad is a giant unit.
points: Derivation: E = σ/ε₀ = Q/(ε₀A), V = Ed = Qd/(ε₀A), so C = Q/V = ε₀A/d.
With C = 1 F and d = 1 cm, A = Cd/ε₀ ≈ 1.1 × 10⁹ m², a square about 33 km on each side. Real capacitors are in µF to pF.
With a dielectric filling the gap (charge fixed), the field becomes E₀/K and V becomes V₀/K.
So C = Kε₀A/d = KC₀. Dielectric constant K = ε/ε₀ (relative permittivity) is greater than 1; ε = Kε₀ is the permittivity of the medium. In terms of susceptibility, K = 1 + χe/ε₀.
Typical K values: vacuum 1, air about 1.0006, water about 80, mica about 6, glass 5 to 10.

example.q: A parallel plate capacitor has A = 0.02 m² and d = 1.77 mm, in air. Find C, and C when mica (K = 6) fills the gap. (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
example.answer: 100 pF in air; 600 pF with mica

learn.reallife: Touchscreens on phones sold across India work as tiny capacitors: your finger, which is mostly water with high permittivity, changes the local capacitance and the phone senses where you touched.

revise.summary: For a parallel plate capacitor C = ε₀A/d; one farad needs an enormous area. A dielectric of constant K = ε/ε₀ filling the gap multiplies C by K and, at fixed charge, divides E and V by K.
focus: Effect of a dielectric at fixed charge
remember: C = ε₀A/d; with dielectric C = KC₀
Fixed Q: E → E₀/K, V → V₀/K
traps: C ∝ 1/d, not d
The farad is a very large unit

learn.hook: An Indian electronics hobbyist with only 2 µF capacitors can still make 1 µF, 3 µF or 4 µF. The trick is combining them in series and parallel.
points: Series: each capacitor carries the same charge Q; voltages add. 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + ... (C is less than the smallest).
Parallel: each capacitor has the same voltage V; charges add. C = C₁ + C₂ + ... (C is more than the largest).
Two in series: C = C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂). n equal capacitors C: series gives C/n, parallel gives nC.
Slab of thickness t (< d) with constant K: C = ε₀A/(d - t + t/K). A metal slab (K → ∞) gives C = ε₀A/(d - t).
To build a required C and voltage rating, put capacitors in series to share the voltage, and parallel rows to increase C.

example.q: A 3 µF and a 6 µF capacitor are in series across 90 V. Find the equivalent capacitance, the charge and the voltage on each.
example.answer: C = 2 µF; Q = 180 µC each; 60 V on 3 µF and 30 V on 6 µF

learn.reallife: Power-factor capacitor banks in Indian factories are built by wiring many capacitors in series-parallel groups so that the bank can handle the 11 kV supply and still give the needed capacitance.

teach.ask: Gappu has two capacitors and asks: 'Which way of joining them gives a bigger total?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Parallel capacitors add directly with the same voltage; series capacitors share the same charge and give less. Yay!
teach.nudge: Nice! Which arrangement adds capacitances directly, and what is common to each in series?

revise.summary: In series, capacitors share the same charge and 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + …; in parallel they share the same voltage and C = C₁ + C₂ + …. A partial slab gives C = ε₀A/(d − t + t/K).
focus: Capacitor with partial dielectric or metal slab
remember: Series: same Q; 1/C = Σ1/Cᵢ; n equal → C/n
Parallel: same V; C = ΣCᵢ; n equal → nC
Slab: C = ε₀A/(d − t + t/K); metal: ε₀A/(d − t)
traps: In series the smaller capacitor does not take the smaller voltage; it takes the larger one
Don't add series capacitances directly

learn.hook: Defibrillators in Indian ambulances store around 200 J in a capacitor and dump it into a patient's heart in milliseconds to restore its rhythm.
points: Energy stored: U = Q²/2C = ½CV² = ½QV. It is the work done in charging the capacitor.
The energy is stored in the electric field between the plates, with energy density u = ½ε₀E² (per unit volume). With a dielectric, u = ½Kε₀E².

Connecting a charged capacitor to an uncharged one: charge is shared until both reach a common potential V = (C₁V₁ + C₂V₂)/(C₁ + C₂). Some energy is always lost as heat and radiation in the connecting wires.
Dielectric inserted with battery connected: V fixed, C → KC, Q → KQ, U → KU.
Dielectric inserted after disconnecting: Q fixed, C → KC, V → V/K, U → U/K.

example.q: A 10 µF capacitor is charged to 100 V and then connected to an uncharged 10 µF capacitor. Find the energy before and after.
steps: U₂ = ½ × 20 × 10⁻⁶ × 2500 = 0.025 J; half the energy is lost

teach.praise: Chirp! It is stored in the electric field between the plates, ½CV² in total. Energy in empty space, cool!

revise.summary: A capacitor stores U = Q²/2C = ½CV² = ½QV in its field, with energy density ½ε₀E². Sharing charge between capacitors always loses energy; with a battery connected a dielectric raises U by K, but when isolated it lowers U by K.
focus: Charge sharing and dielectric insertion cases
remember: Battery on: U → KU; isolated: U → U/K
traps: Energy is not conserved in charge sharing; some is lost
Don't apply K before deciding whether Q or V is fixed
